title: Decide whether to trust the report
subtitle: Check the answer. Read the evidence. Make a reasoned decision.
courseLabel: Harness in practice · Tutorial 4 of 6 · Verify → Review
coursePath: Turn an idea into a useful result
Decide whether to trust the report
Make it work for your needs

sections.title: Decide what makes this report trustworthy
sections.intro: A useful report gives you an answer you can explain, together with evidence for the parts you cannot check by eye.
sections.html:
Click Open formatted report. Find its date range, entry count and total. This is the six-row example used by the current course.

Then ask: what supports those numbers, and what remains uncertain?

By the end of this lesson, you will compare the report with its input, distinguish a software-check result from your judgment and write a bounded review decision. Reading these files makes no model call.

Keep the current software-check record beside the report so its commands, source and environment can be inspected.
presenterNotes: Open the actual current-course report. Inspect its numbers rather than relying on a screenshot.
The benefit is explaining why a result is supported and naming its limits.

sections.title: Check one answer yourself
sections.intro: The six-row fixture is small enough to audit without reading the implementation.
sections.html:
Read the supplied CSV. Add its minutes: 90 + 30 + 45 + 60 + 30 + 15 = 270.

Independent totals from the six supplied rows
GroupingExpected totals
ProjectOrion 180; Lumen 90
CategoryDevelopment 150; Documentation 75; Testing 45
Whole report6 entries; 270 minutes; 19–21 October 2026

The project totals and category totals each add to 270. They describe the same work grouped in two ways; adding both tables together would count every minute twice.

Choose one group and explain how its rows produce the expected subtotal. Compare it with the expected text report and the formatted report.

This optional note is saved in local browser storage when available. It is not a Harness result or approval.
presenterNotes: Let the learner calculate one subtotal. Do not replace the activity with a recital of the answer.
The CSV and expected report are primary artifacts; the table is derived from their six rows.

sections.title: Read the recorded result within its scope
sections.intro: A check is useful when you can identify the input, expected answer, command and actual result.
sections.html:
Read the Current software-check record. Find the selected runtime/source, reporting files, actual commands, environment and recorded outcome. Check what ran and whether anything failed, skipped or remained unexecuted.

Connect each claim with evidence
Claim to assessEvidence to inspect
The sample total is 270 minutes.The six CSV rows, independent arithmetic and actual report output.
The text and HTML agree.The current generated outputs and the checks comparing their entries and totals.
An existing report is preserved.The output-file check and its actual result for an existing destination.
The implementation meets the selected checks.The executed test command and recorded pass, failure and skip outcomes.

The current bundled-report test run passed 77 checks, with no failures or skips. Read Text checks and HTML checks when you want to understand an expectation. That result supports the cases it exercised; it does not prove every possible input.

Read this prompt before sending it. It requests inspection only.

copies.label: evidence inspection prompt
copies.text: Inspect the current reporting source, six-row CSV, expected report and current-checks.json. Explain which commands actually ran, what their results establish, what failed or skipped and which claims remain unverified. Separate independent arithmetic, executed checks and your interpretation. Keep the inspection read-only. Do not start a model, change files, approve work or rerun anything merely because a result is uncertain.

presenterNotes: Use the fresh current-checks.json that accompanies this course. Do not import a result from another runtime or source.
The current record reports 77 reporting tests in a fresh Python 3.12 environment. Keep its exact source, environment and result with the course.

sections.title: Turn a concern into a checkable question
sections.intro: A plausible concern deserves a concrete input and expected result before you decide whether it is a defect.
sections.html:
Illustrative concern: a missing row

Suppose a report omitted the final 15-minute Orion testing entry. This is a proposed counterexample for learning, not an observed finding in the current software.

  1. Identify the exact input: the unchanged six-row CSV.
  2. State the independent expectation: 6 entries, 270 minutes and Orion at 180.
  3. Describe the supposed failure: 5 entries, 255 minutes and Orion at 165.
  4. Ask whether current output or a suitable test actually shows that mismatch. Keep the concern unconfirmed until the evidence exists.

If a mismatch is observed, retain the failing input/output and choose a bounded investigation or correction. If it is not observed, report that outcome. A suggestion does not become a bug because it sounds reasonable.
presenterNotes: Label the missing-row case as illustrative. Do not attribute it to a reviewer or an actual run.
Ask what evidence would change the learner’s decision.

sections.title: Handle a real finding without changing the answer
sections.intro: When evidence establishes a defect, preserve the expectation and make the correction inspectable.
sections.html:
Use the missing-row concern as a paper exercise. Decide what a repair task would need before authorizing it:

  1. Keep the six-row input and independently derived expected totals.
  2. Prepare a focused check that exposes an observed mismatch. Verify it against the failing behavior before treating it as a regression check.
  3. Define the smallest allowed implementation change and protect the acceptance expectation from the repair worker.
  4. After separately authorized work, inspect the same check, actual diff and broader relevant results. Preserve failed attempts and any remaining concerns.

Filled proposed response

Trigger: a reproduced missing-row failure, if found.

Expected answer: all six entries remain counted; the total is 270 minutes.

Review point: inspect the input, failure, allowed file scope and independent check before starting a correction.

Current state: this lesson has proposed a response; it has not established a defect or performed a repair.
presenterNotes: Keep a hypothetical repair separate from the current software-check result.
Changing the expected answer changes the contract; it is not a shortcut to green tests.

sections.title: Notice when a plausible total is wrong
sections.intro: The omitted-row example lets you practice checking a result with fewer hints.
sections.html:
If the final 15-minute testing row were omitted, the report would show 5 entries and 255 minutes. Orion would total 165 and Testing 30; Lumen would remain at 90. These numbers could look plausible until compared with the complete input.

  1. Identify the omitted row in the six-row fixture.
  2. Recalculate one affected subtotal.
  3. Explain which check would expose the omission: entry count, grand total, project total or category total.
  4. State what your check would leave untested, such as invalid input or output-file handling.

Use an independent expected answer. Asking the same implementation to produce its own expected total can repeat the same mistake.
presenterNotes: Keep the optional check nonblocking. Invite an explanation rather than merely choosing an option.
The omitted-row numbers are independently calculated expectations, not a software failure report.

check.question: The sample matches the six-row arithmetic and its selected checks pass. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: The recorded checks support the sample and tested cases within the stated source and environment; other behavior may still need evidence.
options.feedback: Correct. Connect the conclusion to the actual checks and keep untested cases visible.

options.text: Every possible input, platform and future change is now proven correct.
options.feedback: The evidence covers the selected inputs, cases, source and environment. Broader claims need their own checks.

sections.title: Leave an explanation another person can inspect
sections.intro: Use a short note to connect the useful result, checked claims and next decision.
sections.html:
Filled review decision

Useful result: the sample accounts for six entries and 270 minutes. Orion totals 180 and Lumen 90; categories total Development 150, Documentation 75 and Testing 45.

Evidence to retain: the input, actual report and current software-check record with source, commands, environment and outcomes.

Concern considered: a missing 15-minute row was an illustrative counterexample, not a confirmed defect.

Decision: accept only claims supported by the inspected current results. Investigate an actual mismatch before authorizing a correction.

Limit: sample agreement and selected tests do not establish every input or platform.

Your wording stays in local browser notes when storage is available. It does not alter a Harness record.
